## Proof

**Answer-leak check:** The problem statement contains only the problem and constraints; no solution, answer, or proof sketch is leaked. Proceeding.

---

Let us introduce the substitution
$$p=\frac{bc^{2}}{a},\qquad q=\frac{ca^{2}}{b},\qquad r=\frac{ab^{2}}{c}.$$

Since $a,b,c>0$ and the constraints give $a\ge bc^{2},\; b\ge ca^{2},\; c\ge ab^{2}$, we have
$$0<p\le 1,\qquad 0<q\le 1,\qquad 0<r\le 1.$$

**Consistency of the parametrization.** Taking logarithms $A=\ln a,\,B=\ln b,\,C=\ln c$, the system becomes
$$-A+B+2C=\ln p,\quad 2A-B+C=\ln q,\quad A+2B-C=\ln r.$$
The coefficient matrix has determinant
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&2\\2&-1&1\\1&2&-1\end{pmatrix}=14\neq 0,$$
so for every $(p,q,r)$ with $p,q,r>0$ there exists a unique $(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c>0$. Hence the parametrization is bijective onto the feasible region, and maximizing $E$ over the feasible $(a,b,c)$ is equivalent to maximizing over $(p,q,r)\in(0,1]^{3}$.

**Rewriting $E$.** Note that
$$a-bc^{2}=a(1-p),\qquad b-ca^{2}=b(1-q),\qquad c-ab^{2}=c(1-r),$$
and
$$pqr=\frac{bc^{2}}{a}\cdot\frac{ca^{2}}{b}\cdot\frac{ab^{2}}{c}=a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}=(abc)^{2}.$$
Therefore
$$E=abc\cdot a(1-p)\cdot b(1-q)\cdot c(1-r)=(abc)^{2}(1-p)(1-q)(1-r)=pqr(1-p)(1-q)(1-r).$$
This factors completely as
$$E=\bigl[p(1-p)\bigr]\bigl[q(1-q)\bigr]\bigl[r(1-r)\bigr].$$

**Bounding each factor.** For any $t\in(0,1]$,
$$t(1-t)\le \frac{1}{4},$$
with equality if and only if $t=\tfrac12$ (the vertex of the parabola, which lies in $(0,1]$). Hence
$$E\le \left(\frac14\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{64}.$$

**Equality is attained.** Take $p=q=r=\tfrac12$. By symmetry of the system, the solution is $a=b=c=t$ with $t^{2}=bc^{2}/a=t^{2}\cdot t/t$... more directly, $p=bc^{2}/a=t^{3}/t=t^{2}=\tfrac12$, so $t=1/\sqrt2$. Then
$$E=t^{6}(1-t^{2})^{3}=\left(\frac12\right)^{3}\left(\frac12\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{64},$$
and the constraints $t\ge t^{3}$ hold since $t^{2}=\tfrac12<1$.

Therefore the maximum value of $E$ is

$$\boxed{\dfrac{1}{64}}.$$
